header.tag_why: The deal moved from what the rep called dead to signed after Wen built a cost figure from the customer's own statements and Ines said "that's my number, not yours"; the payout reconciliation capability got her attention, but her own number closed it.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: For finance-led buyers who sell domestically, open with reconciliation in the buyer's words, not global growth: "Know where every deposit came from. Each payout reconciles automatically to its transactions and your ERP, so month-end stops being a week of archaeology." Lead the first call with the payout reconciliation demo, and offer to run it on the buyer's own data.
messaging_changes.why: The "Financial infrastructure, global growth, all the currencies" opener got silence from a business that sells "to restaurants in three states." The only reaction came from payout reconciliation, and the CFO's own words were "the deposits" and "I just want to know where my money is."

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: For finance buyers, replace the third-party study with an offer to build their number: "Send us one month of your statements and we'll show you what reconciliation costs you today, in your numbers, not ours." Reuse the method only. Do not quote hours or dollar figures from other deals.
messaging_changes.why: The deal turned when a cost model was built from one month of the controller's statements and the CFO said "that's my number, not yours," after she had already asked to see it with their data.

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: When the economic buyer is in finance and IT isn't building anything, stop leading proposals and first calls with APIs, docs and sandbox. Write page one for the finance decider in finance terms (close time, unmatched deposits), and move checkout and API detail to an appendix.
messaging_changes.why: The first proposal was "all about the portal. The checkout, the APIs." The deciding CFO read the first page and said it wasn't her problem, the deal stalled three weeks, and the IT team "aren't building anything."

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: Add a wholesale/distributor reference (invoice-based business) that can take a peer call with a finance buyer. For distributor prospects, offer that reference instead of retail stories, and close the request before signature.
messaging_changes.why: The CFO asked to talk to another distributor and dismissed the retail story with "this is a company that sells sweaters." We never got her a call, and she brought it up twice.

trigger.insight: The inbound named a portal project, but the money and urgency came from a new CFO whose first close took nine days of manual three-way matching. The rep first said they were building a portal, then said the portal is off the shelf with a plugin. So the stated project never needed what we led with, and it took until about the third call to find the real driver.
trigger.messaging: When an inbound names a channel project at a business with manual finance operations, discovery should ask about month-end close time and reconciliation before we pitch checkout.

decider.insight: The CFO decided, and the IT contact said so plainly. The rep's framing that Ines sat on the proposal hides the real problem: we wrote it for the IT director, and the decider rejected it after one page. The three-week stall was a sign we were talking to the wrong buyer, not slowness on her side.
decider.messaging: Write page one of every proposal for the economic buyer, in finance terms (close time, unmatched deposits), and put APIs and checkout in an appendix.

competitor.insight: According to Ines, the incumbent bank answered her with a rate review, and she rejected that because her problem was visibility, not price. The rep said not much changed after the bank conversation, then described a new question about getting a named contact, prompted by her bank rep changing without her knowing who the new one was. What Fiserv itself pitched is unknown, and the transcript doesn't establish whether the named-contact promise went further than the rep saying yes, me.
competitor.messaging: Against bank-bundled incumbents, don't compete on rates; position support as a named person who knows the account (not M5's tiered response times), next to reconciliation.

message.insight: M1 (global, every currency) and M2 (developers) both fell flat: the business sells in three states and the IT team isn't building anything. Only M9 got a reaction, strong enough that the CFO interrupted the demo and then asked to see it with her own data. Our standard opener spent the first call on the two messages least relevant to this buyer.
message.messaging: For domestic, finance-led buyers, open with M9 (each payout tied to its transactions and the ERP) and drop the global/currency opener entirely.

decided.insight: The turn came from a cost model built on one month of the customer's own statements, not from a generic ROI claim; Ines valued it because the inputs were hers. The rep had the deal at 20 percent even though the CFO had already asked to see it with her data, which was a clear buying signal. The rep's figures (something like 60 hours a month, low six figures a year) are recalled estimates and should not be reused as numbers.
decided.messaging: Replace M6's independent economic impact study with an offer to build the buyer's own cost-of-reconciliation number from one month of their statements.

gaps.insight: We had no wholesale or distributor proof. Sending a retail story backfired, and the gap stayed open through signature. The question about counter card readers at 14 branches landing in the same report was answered with a slide and no demo, and the transcript doesn't establish whether the branches are in the signed scope. The rep left both out of what they would do differently.
gaps.messaging: Build a distributor/wholesale reference for M8, and frame M3 for this buyer as counter sales and online orders reconciled in one report, backed by a demo rather than a slide.

language.insight: The buyer talks about deposits, month-end and where her money is. We talk about payments, infrastructure and growth. Her problem is not knowing where her money is, and our opener promised more of what she already couldn't track.
language.messaging: Use her vocabulary in finance-buyer messaging: know where every deposit came from, and close the month without the archaeology, instead of financial infrastructure.

gaps.question: Are the 14 branches' counter card readers in the signed scope, or only the online portal?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana (and check the signed order form): did the contract include in-store/counter processing, or are branches still on Fiserv through the bank?

gaps.question: What did Fiserv or the bank actually show or offer?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana to ask Ines or Paul whether the bank came back with anything beyond the rate review, and what it was.

gaps.question: What changed in their questions after they talked to the bank?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana: is the named-contact commitment written into the contract or a support plan, or is it only Dana's personal promise?

gaps.question: What were the exact hours and dollar figure in the cost model?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Wen for the actual model built from the controller's statements, so the method (not the rep's estimate) can be reused.

gaps.question: Anything you'd do differently?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana what would have closed the distributor-reference gap Ines raised twice, and whether a branch reader demo was ever offered.

close.rep_takeaway: You won this when you stopped pitching and started using her numbers. Make that the first move, not the rescue: ask in the first call who owns the pain and what it costs them. Treat a request to see it with their own data as the strongest buying signal there is, not a 20 percent deal. And when a buyer asks for something twice, like a distributor reference, close it before signature, because it will come back at renewal.
